evidence.quote: We found the following cortical regions were activated robustly (voxelwise false discovery rate = 1%): lateral premotor cortex; dorsal cingulate and medial premotor cortex; dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex; frontal poles; and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex.
evidence.cite: Owen AM, McMillan KM, Laird AR, et al. N-back working memory paradigm: a meta-analysis of normative functional neuroimaging studies. Hum Brain Mapp. 2005;25(1):46-59.

evidence.claim: Dorsolateral lesions produce executive dysfunction
evidence.finding: The authors compared 19 patients with dorsolateral prefrontal lesions, 152 with other lesions and 54 without brain lesions on working memory and reasoning tests. Dorsolateral damage was associated with deficits in manipulating verbal and spatial knowledge. The left side was needed for manipulating information in working memory, and the right side for a broader range of reasoning.
evidence.quote: DlPFC damage was associated with deficits in the manipulation of verbal and spatial knowledge, with left dlPFC necessary for manipulating information in working memory and right dlPFC critical for manipulating information in a broader range of reasoning contexts.
evidence.cite: Barbey AK, Koenigs M, Grafman J. Dorsolateral prefrontal contributions to human working memory. Cortex. 2013;49(5):1195-205.

evidence.claim: Its posterior end contains the frontal eye field, which drives voluntary saccades
evidence.finding: In 19 awake patients with subdural electrodes for epilepsy surgery, stimulation of the frontal lobe produced eye movements toward the opposite side. The movements were saccadic in 84% and were followed by head turning in 58%, and in most patients the eye fields lay at or in front of the motor representation. The abstract does not name the gyrus, so this supports the frontal eye field described in the entry.
evidence.quote: They were saccadic in 16 patients (84%). Head version, always following the eye deviation, occurred in 11 patients (58%).
evidence.cite: Godoy J, Lüders H, Dinner DS, et al. Versive eye movements elicited by cortical stimulation of the human brain. Neurology. 1990;40(2):296-9.

data.title: Eye movements evoked by stimulation (19 patients)

stimulation.method: subdural electrode stimulation in awake epilepsy patients
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the frontal eye field region in front of the motor strip made the eyes move to the opposite side, usually in jerks (saccades), often with the head turning after them.
stimulation.quote: They were saccadic in 16 patients (84%). Head version, always following the eye deviation, occurred in 11 patients (58%).
stimulation.cite: Godoy J, Lüders H, Dinner DS, et al. Versive eye movements elicited by cortical stimulation of the human brain. Neurology. 1990;40(2):296-9.

how_we_know: The face area was found with fMRI, which is correlational. Stimulation through intracranial electrodes in epilepsy patients tests cause, and lesion reviews show which damage produces prosopagnosia and achromatopsia. Whether the face area is specific to faces or reflects expertise is still debated.

evidence.claim: The mid-fusiform part contains the fusiform face area, which responds strongly to faces
evidence.finding: Using fMRI, the authors found an area in the fusiform gyrus in 12 of the 15 people tested that was more active for faces than for common objects. In follow-up tests, this area also responded more to intact than scrambled faces and to faces than to houses or hands. They concluded it is selectively involved in face perception.
evidence.quote: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we found an area in the fusiform gyrus in 12 of the 15 subjects tested that was significantly more active when the subjects viewed faces than when they viewed assorted common objects.
evidence.cite: Kanwisher N, McDermott J, Chun MM. The fusiform face area: a module in human extrastriate cortex specialized for face perception. J Neurosci. 1997;17(11):4302-11.

evidence.claim: Damage to the right or both fusiform gyri causes prosopagnosia
evidence.finding: Ten epilepsy patients with intracranial electrodes in the left (5 patients, 30 sites) or right (5 patients, 26 sites) fusiform gyrus were tested. Face-selective recordings occurred on both sides, but only stimulation of the right fusiform gyrus changed the conscious perception of faces. Stimulating strongly face-selective left sites caused non-face visual changes such as phosphenes.
evidence.quote: Only EBS of the right FG caused changes in the conscious perception of faces, whereas EBS of strongly face-selective regions in the left FG produced non-face-related visual changes, such as phosphenes.
evidence.cite: Rangarajan V, Hermes D, Foster BL, et al. Electrical stimulation of the left and right human fusiform gyrus causes different effects in conscious face perception. J Neurosci. 2014;34(38):12828-36.

evidence.claim: Damage near this gyrus can cause achromatopsia, loss of color vision
evidence.finding: The authors pooled 92 published case reports of cerebral achromatopsia. The lesions overlapped most in a small region of ventral occipital cortex, near areas that imaging links to color perception. A similar analysis of prosopagnosia found several regions of high lesion overlap beside it.
evidence.quote: Lesion overlap analyses revealed a relatively small region of high overlap in ventral occipital cortex.
evidence.cite: Bouvier SE, Engel SA. Behavioral deficits and cortical damage loci in cerebral achromatopsia. Cereb Cortex. 2006;16(2):183-91.

stimulation.method: intracranial electrical stimulation in an epilepsy patient
stimulation.effect: Stimulating face-selective sites in the right fusiform gyrus made the faces of people in the room look distorted or metamorphosed, while nonface objects looked normal.
stimulation.quote: Moreover, electrical charge delivered to this pair of electrodes induced a profound face-specific perceptual distortion during viewing of real faces.
stimulation.cite: Parvizi J, Jacques C, Foster BL, et al. Electrical stimulation of human fusiform face-selective regions distorts face perception. J Neurosci. 2012;32(43):14915-20.

how_we_know: The place area was found with fMRI, and a rare stimulation case supports its causal role. Alzheimer pathology staging comes from post-mortem staining of thousands of brains. The entorhinal part is covered by the staging data, while the scene-selective part is covered by imaging and stimulation.

evidence.claim: Its posterior part processes scenes and spatial layout and includes the parahippocampal place area
evidence.finding: Using fMRI, the authors found a region in human parahippocampal cortex that responded selectively to passively viewed scenes. It responded weakly to single objects and not at all to faces. Empty rooms drove it as strongly as furnished rooms, so it appears to encode the layout of local space.
evidence.quote: This region, which we name the 'parahippocampal place area' (PPA), responds selectively and automatically in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to passively viewed scenes, but only weakly to single objects and not at all to faces.
evidence.cite: Epstein R, Kanwisher N. A cortical representation of the local visual environment. Nature. 1998;392(6676):598-601.

evidence.claim: A scene-selective area in this region processes scenes and spatial layout
evidence.finding: In one epilepsy patient, fMRI and intracranial EEG identified a place-selective area in the collateral sulcus and medial fusiform gyrus. Electrical stimulation of that area caused a visual hallucination of indoor and outdoor scenes. Stimulating the more lateral basal temporal cortex instead distorted faces.
evidence.quote: Bipolar direct electrical stimulation of a cortical area in the collateral sulcus and medial fusiform gyrus, which was place-selective according to both fMRI and iEEG, induced a topographic visual hallucination: the patient described seeing indoor and outdoor scenes that included views of the neighborhood he lives in.
evidence.cite: Mégevand P, Groppe DM, Goldfinger MS, et al. Seeing scenes: topographic visual hallucinations evoked by direct electrical stimulation of the parahippocampal place area. J Neurosci. 2014;34(16):5399-405.

evidence.claim: Neurofibrillary tangles appear first in the entorhinal cortex in Alzheimer disease
evidence.finding: The authors stained 2332 brains from people aged 1 to 100 years for abnormal tau. Among cortical areas, abnormal tau appeared first in the transentorhinal region (Stage 1a, 38 cases), at the border of the entorhinal region. They also found tau in the locus coeruleus before any cortical involvement.
evidence.quote: Cortical involvement (abnormal tau in neurites) was identified first in the transentorhinal region (Stage 1a, 38 cases).
evidence.cite: Braak H, Thal DR, Ghebremedhin E, Del Tredici K. Stages of the pathologic process in Alzheimer disease: age categories from 1 to 100 years. J Neuropathol Exp Neurol. 2011;70(11):960-9.

stimulation.method: direct electrical stimulation with intracranial electrodes (single patient)
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the place-selective area in the collateral sulcus and medial fusiform gyrus made the patient see indoor and outdoor scenes, including views of his own neighborhood.
stimulation.quote: Bipolar direct electrical stimulation of a cortical area in the collateral sulcus and medial fusiform gyrus, which was place-selective according to both fMRI and iEEG, induced a topographic visual hallucination: the patient described seeing indoor and outdoor scenes that included views of the neighborhood he lives in.
stimulation.cite: Mégevand P, Groppe DM, Goldfinger MS, et al. Seeing scenes: topographic visual hallucinations evoked by direct electrical stimulation of the parahippocampal place area. J Neurosci. 2014;34(16):5399-405.
